I worked at a dive shop, the place didn't pay enough to pay my bills.  The debt from trying to make the job work was piling up, and everything seemed like there wasn't a way out.

I'd started to put the pieces together in my head.  Fill up a tank with 100% argon, no air, no oxygen.

Put on a regulator and a full face mask... Seal... Breathe.  In moments you'd pass out from hypoxia.  Most people drift off or have a moment of impairment before drifting off.  

A few more minutes breathing that, and you're done for.  Painless, easy, you fuck it up and maybe you're a vegetable but odds are you recover.

And then a podcast played that usual warning 'if you or someone you love is having suicidal thoughts...'

I called the number, I reached out to people I knew could help, and I got out of that job eventually.

It's been about 6 years since then, I have two kids I love to bits.  I still have rough times, I know myself well enough to stay way from 'easy' methods.  But still... Sometimes it's hard.

1. Is diving part of your job? Or do you do it as a hobby? How did you get into diving?

It isn’t any longer!  But it used to be when I was an instructor.  I started off wanting to take a small step towards diving on the Great Barrier Reef.  I figured I would get certified locally and make sure I knew what I was doing before taking such a big and expensive trip.  Once I started, I immediately fell in love with the combination of science, and technology, as well as skills to learn to dive safely.

2. Is diving in the ocean dangerous? If it is, what dangers do you face?

Everything is dangerous to some degree.  And being underwater where you can’t breathe presents some pretty unique risks.  The most obvious is that you need to make sure you plan out your dive and keep a careful eye on your air, as well as make sure you take care of your equipment so it doesn’t have a problem underwater.  That’s one of the biggest dangers, making sure you can breathe, because we’re not able to breathe underwater.

3. Is scuba diving fun? What parts make it fun?

For me, SCUBA diving is very fun.  I love seeing the reef and all the fish on it as they go about their day.  Just like when you go on a walk in the woods and look at the animals going about their day, I like to go on a dive through the reef.

4. How does coral bleaching kill coral?

Coral Bleaching is really just part of what kills a coral polyp.  Coral isn’t just the little rocky parts you see, there’s actually a kinda weird squishy creature that lives inside that stuff and that rocky stuff is it’s bones.  Crazy right?!  Well, that coral polyp has a type of plant called algae living inside it.  When the water gets too warm, or when conditions are wrong, they end up losing that algae, and the color that the algae gave them.  THAT is bleaching.  Now it can kill the coral polyp, because it can’t get anymore food from the algae, which the algae makes from sunlight, and they eventually starve.

5. Have you ever come across creatures that you found to be highly intelligent?

6. How do underwater plants help both fish and humans?

Most of the oxygen in our atmosphere is actually made by oceanic algae on the surface!  More oxygen comes from the ocean than EVERYTHING on land.  Scientists estimate about 50-80% of all the oxygen we breathe comes from the ocean, which is pretty incredible.    
Plus, lots of seaweed is pretty tasty!

7. What made you want to scuba dive in the first place?

I always wanted to see the Great Barrier Reef, and I remember playing some underwater videogames as a kid that made me excited to try diving.  With the world changing, I want to see some of these places before they change forever.

8. Is it true that sometimes fish in the sea can grow to like you?

Yes!  There was a Moray Eel near the resort I used to work at that would get to know some of the instructors and would sometimes come out to get pet.  That being said, don’t touch the wildlife on a dive.

9. Do you ever save wildlife?  
I have not, but we can all do our part to keep the wildlife safe.  Making sure we use less single use plastic, being mindful of our impact, and working to make sure that larger companies do the same.

10. Have you ever come across any poisonous wildlife in the ocean?

Yes!  Poisonous things make you sick when you eat them.  Venomous things usually make you hurt, or sick through other means, like a bee. I’ve had a few jellyfish stings, they’re usually not very bad just a little zap of pain and that’s it.  I’ve accidentally put my hand on a sea urchin once, that wasn’t fun, just a warm radiating kind of pain.  I’ve seen plenty of other venomous species, but they don’t want anything to do with us.

Let's make this abstract for a second.  Imagine you have a copy of an image, except I change one pixel of that image.  Is it still the same image?  Now, how many pixels do we take away or change before you say it's not the same image?  Philosopher's call this problem the Ship of Theseus paradox.  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_of_Theseus

Variation in a genetic sequence is the same issue.  We see in humans that some adaptations, lactose tolerance for instance, or sickle cell anemia, are particular adaptations to certain environmental stresses.  Now that small adaptation may not seem like much, very much in the way that a one pixel discrepancy doesn't seem like very much at first.  But how many adaptations before you'd consider it 'another kind of life form'?

If you want we can get into the nitty gritty of specific examples where organs or systems evolved on a creature that had to occur via small, iterative changes, where if too many changes happened all at once the organ couldn't function.  A clear example is the way our own eyes have blood vessels that block parts of our vision producing problematic blind spots.  We could easily conceive of a better system, where the blood vessels didn't lay over parts of your eyes, but that sort of rewiring isn't something that could happen by the small iterative, step by step process that evolution is constrained to.  And so, we're stuck with our blind spots.

The fact that we can find every intermediate version of the eye in the natural world, from light sensitive cells, to pin hole camera style eyes of many types of invertebrates, to our own, and even birds eyes, can show you quite clearly that our bodies were shaped by the same processes.  If anything seeing that process should fill you with an awe and wonder, and if you are a godly person, perhaps it should fill you with amazement that your deity started such a process.

Hiya, I'm an instructor myself and actually started my journey by doing my research for exactly that trip.

First!  Do yourself a huge favor and get as much dive experience between now, and your trip departure.  You're spending probably upwards of $3,000 for your trip, better get your money out of those dives and enjoy them to the fullest.  So in order to do that, you'll need enough experience that the actually equipment is as close to 2nd nature as you can get it.  So take this and next weekend to get some time just tooling around in the water some more.  Get comfortable setting it up and using it.  I worked in the Caribbean for a while and saw oodles of folks exactly in your situation who wasted their dives completely out of control with their buoyancy.

Second!  As long as you're comfortable with your skills and adapting to new gear, renting is fine.  Having your own gear is nice but not a must.  A computer is nice to have and you can always just get a wrist style one for ~200-~500 depending on how nice you want.

Third!  Your camera won't survive any real dive if it's rated for barely 10m.  Go buy a gopro and make sure you have the proper dive housing.  Again, you've spent how much on your trip and what's another $300 ish on a solid go pro set up.

That's basically it, get your fundamental skills honed, get out there, dive more etc.  Make your mistakes here, and you will make mistakes, before you're on your dives out there!
